title: Civil Peace

toc.title: 5.5 Setting, structure and point of view

html:
Chinua Achebe's "Civil Peace" is set in Nigeria in the first weeks after the Nigerian Civil War of 1967–70. Its hero, Jonathan Iwegbu, has lost a son, a job and almost everything he owned, and still insists that he is an extraordinarily lucky man. The story is on the syllabus because it shows, in very few pages, what ordinary people do after a war ends — and how little the word "peace" may actually mean to them.

The central idea

The war is over but the violence is not. What has changed is only its name. Against that, Achebe sets Jonathan's stubborn, practical, almost comic determination to survive, count his blessings and begin again.

5.1 About the author

Chinua Albert Chinualumogu Achebe (1930–2013) was a Nigerian novelist, poet, short story writer and essayist, and is usually called the father of modern African literature written in English. He was born at Ogidi in eastern Nigeria, into an Igbo family; his parents were Christian converts, but the traditional life of the village went on around him, and that double inheritance runs through all his work. He studied at University College, Ibadan, and afterwards worked for the Nigerian Broadcasting Service.

His first novel, Things Fall Apart (1958), is the most widely read African novel ever written; it was followed by No Longer at Ease (1960), Arrow of God (1964), A Man of the People (1966) and, much later, Anthills of the Savannah (1987). He also wrote a famous essay attacking Joseph Conrad's picture of Africa in Heart of Darkness. When the eastern region of Nigeria broke away in 1967 as the Republic of Biafra, Achebe supported it and travelled abroad on its behalf; the war that followed killed perhaps a million people, mostly of hunger, and it is out of that experience that the stories in Girls at War and Other Stories (1972) — which contains "Civil Peace" — were written. A car accident in 1990 left him unable to walk, and he spent his last years teaching in the United States. He died in 2013.

Biafra and the Nigerian Civil War

In 1967 the mainly Igbo eastern region of Nigeria declared itself the independent state of Biafra. The federal government fought to prevent this. The war lasted from 1967 to January 1970 and ended in Biafra's defeat, after a blockade that caused mass starvation. "Civil Peace" begins immediately after the surrender.

What is distinctive about Achebe's voice is its calm. He writes about catastrophe in clear, unexcited sentences and lets the facts do the work. He gives his characters their own English — here, the Nigerian Pidgin of the thieves and of Jonathan himself — and he refuses to make his people either saints or victims. The result is irony rather than protest: he shows you the situation and trusts you to judge it.

5.2 The story

A lucky man. The story opens with Jonathan Iwegbu deciding that he has been extraordinarily lucky. The war is over. He has come through it with what he calls five "inestimable blessings": his own head, his wife Maria's head, and the heads of three of his four children. The missing child is mentioned in the same sentence as the others, without a pause for grief, and that flat arithmetic tells us how much death there has been. Whenever anything happens to him, good or bad, Jonathan says the same thing: "Nothing puzzles God."

The bicycle. His sixth blessing is his old bicycle. During the war a Biafran officer in a war-time uniform had tried to commandeer it for military use; Jonathan, certain the man was no real officer, argued, then quietly paid him two pounds, and the bicycle was released. Jonathan then buried it in the ground, wrapped up, and dug it out after the fighting stopped to find it in working order. He at once turned it into a taxi, carrying people and goods between the camps and the military cemetery, and in two weeks he made a hundred and fifteen pounds — a small fortune in a destroyed country.

The house. With that money he took his family back to Enugu, expecting to find nothing. Instead his little zinc-roofed house in Ogui Overside was still standing, though houses far more solid than his lay in rubble all around it. It needed only a few nails, some wire and some cardboard; he found a carpenter, a man as desperate as himself, who did the repairs for a small payment, and the family moved back in.

Everyone works. The whole household then sets about earning. The children pick mangoes and sell them to soldiers' wives. Maria makes and sells breakfast balls of fried bean paste — akara — to her neighbours. Jonathan finds that his old job at the coal mine no longer exists: the office is open, but no one can tell him when or whether the mines will reopen, so after a few visits he stops wasting his time and opens a bar in his house instead, selling palm-wine to soldiers and to the few other people with money. Achebe is careful to show that survival here is a family business, not the achievement of one clever man.

The ex-gratia award. Then comes the egg-rasher. Biafran currency is now worthless, and anyone who hands it in at the treasury receives a flat "ex-gratia award" of twenty pounds — which the crowd, unable to manage the Latin phrase, pronounces "egg-rasher". Jonathan queues for his, and Achebe fills the scene with anxiety: people pushed together, rumours, and one man who is robbed of his money the moment he has collected it. Jonathan, clutching his twenty pounds, gets home safely and, for once, does not sleep well.

The thieves. That night the family is woken by loud knocking and a voice calling politely to the owner of the house. Jonathan and his family begin to shout "Thief! Thief!" into the darkness, calling for neighbours, for police, for soldiers. Nobody comes. Then, in the most frightening moment in the story, the leader of the thieves joins in and shouts for police and neighbours himself, mockingly, to prove that no help exists. He tells Jonathan that the war is over and that there is no need for anybody to be hurt: "No Civil War again. This time na Civil Peace." He wants one hundred pounds, and says that he knows Jonathan has just collected his award. He offers, almost courteously, to go away if the money is handed out, and even to provide a guard afterwards.

The bargain. Jonathan opens the door and pleads. He has no hundred pounds; he has only the twenty from the treasury, and they may have it. He hands over the whole egg-rasher. The thieves take it, wish the family a good night, and go.

The morning after. At daybreak the neighbours arrive to sympathise. They find Jonathan already at work, palm-wine kegs being loaded, Maria frying her akara, the children on their way to the mango trees. He tells them not to trouble themselves. The money came to him from nowhere a week ago, so losing it means nothing, and anyway, he says once more, "Nothing puzzles God."

5.3 Characters

Character Who they are Role in the story
Jonathan Iwegbu A former coal-mine worker in Enugu; husband, father, owner of a bicycle The protagonist: practical, cheerful, religious, endlessly adaptable
Maria Jonathan's wife Works beside him; makes and sells akara; screams for help with the family
The three surviving children Unnamed; the fourth child died in the war Pick and sell mangoes; part of the family's survival economy
The leader of the thieves An unnamed man who speaks Pidgin English, polite and utterly without fear The antagonist, and the voice of the story's title
The Biafran officer Tried to commandeer the bicycle during the war Shows that robbery in uniform came before robbery in the dark
The neighbours People of Ogui Overside Their silence at night, and their sympathy in the morning, measure the state of society

Jonathan Iwegbu. He is one of the great survivors in modern fiction, and Achebe builds him out of actions rather than feelings. Notice what he actually does: he bribes an officer rather than argue to the end; he buries his bicycle; he digs it up and immediately turns it into income; he stops going to the mine office the moment he sees that the job is gone; he repairs a house with wire and cardboard; he puts his wife and children to work; he gives the thieves everything he has rather than risk a life. Every one of these is a decision to accept the world as it is and act. His religion is part of the same practicality — "Nothing puzzles God" is not deep theology but a way of refusing to be destroyed by what he cannot control. Whether we admire this or find it disturbing is the question the story leaves open. He counts his dead child among his blessings because three of four survived; that is either courage or numbness, and Achebe will not tell us which.

Maria. She has few lines but she is never a decoration. She cooks akara before dawn and sells it; she is with Jonathan in the dark, shouting for help; and she is back at her frying the next morning. Achebe uses her to make the point that the family survives as a unit, and that the labour is shared.

The leader of the thieves. He is the most chilling character because he is so reasonable. He does not break down the door; he knocks and calls politely. He does not deny that he is a thief. When the family cries for help, he takes up the cry himself to demonstrate that no help will come — a piece of theatre that tells Jonathan more about his country than any speech could. And it is he, not the narrator, who names the story: the war has ended, so this is "Civil Peace". He represents a society in which authority has collapsed and the only remaining rule is that the armed take from the unarmed.

5.4 Themes

Peace in name only. The title is the theme. Achebe sets the whole story in the weeks after a formal surrender and then shows a family being robbed at gunpoint while the neighbours, police and soldiers stay silent. The thief's own phrase — "No Civil War again. This time na Civil Peace" — makes the irony explicit. For ordinary Nigerians, the difference between civil war and civil peace is a change of vocabulary, not of danger.

Survival, adaptability and work. The story is full of small, concrete acts of recovery: the buried bicycle, the taxi service, the cardboard and wire, the mangoes, the akara, the palm-wine bar. Achebe's respect goes to people who do not wait to be rescued. Jonathan's genius is that he never mourns a loss longer than it takes to find the next opportunity.

Loss and the value of a human life. Behind the cheerfulness the story is full of death. A son is gone. The bicycle earns its money by carrying people to and from a military cemetery. Jonathan's list of blessings is literally a count of heads, because in that war heads were what people lost. The comedy of the story sits on top of a very large grave, and the reader is meant to feel both at once.

Faith and fatalism. "Nothing puzzles God" is repeated at the start of the story and again at the very end, after the robbery. It is Jonathan's whole philosophy: what comes, comes, and complaining changes nothing. Read positively, this faith is what keeps him working and sane. Read critically, it is the attitude that allows injustice to continue, because nobody demands an explanation.

The breakdown of law and community. The most frightening fact in "Civil Peace" is not the thieves but the silence. Jonathan's family shout into the night for neighbours, police and soldiers, and the only answer is the thief's mocking echo. Yet the same neighbours come at daybreak to sympathise. Achebe is describing a community that still feels for one another but can no longer protect one another.

5.5 Setting, structure and point of view

Setting. Enugu, in eastern Nigeria, in the weeks immediately following the end of the civil war in January 1970. The details are exact and they all carry meaning: the zinc-roofed house standing among rubble, the military cemetery, the closed coal mine, the treasury queue, the worthless Biafran currency. The time is the crucial part of the setting. This is the moment when a country announces that normal life has resumed, and the story asks what that announcement is worth.

Structure. The story has two clearly marked halves. The first is a rapid, almost cheerful account of recovery — blessings, bicycle, house, jobs, money. The second is a single night scene of about half the story's length, in which the thieves arrive. Achebe lets the first half build our confidence in Jonathan's luck so that the robbery lands hard. The ending then returns us, in a few lines, to exactly where we began: a working family and the sentence "Nothing puzzles God." This circular shape is the point. Nothing Jonathan can do changes the conditions he lives in; all he can change is how fast he starts again.

Point of view. Third person, limited to Jonathan. We share his thoughts, his valuations and his ignorance — we never learn who the thieves were, and neither does he. Achebe also keeps his narration close to Jonathan's own speech rhythms, and he writes the thieves' dialogue in Nigerian Pidgin English, so that the difference in voice does part of the characterisation. The narrator never comments on the morality of anything, which is why the irony is so strong.

Irony

Saying or showing one thing while the situation means the opposite. In "Civil Peace" almost everything is ironic: a man who has lost a son calls himself lucky; a robbery is conducted politely; and the word "peace" is spoken by an armed thief.

5.6 Literary devices

Device Example from the text Effect
Irony (situational) A thief announces the arrival of "Civil Peace" The title's meaning is reversed; peace is shown to be only a word
Irony (verbal) Jonathan calls himself "extraordinarily lucky" after losing a child and a job Measures how low expectations have fallen
Refrain / repetition "Nothing puzzles God", spoken at the beginning and at the end Frames the story and defines Jonathan's philosophy
Symbolism The bicycle Buried through the war and dug up after it: the buried, indestructible ability to start again
Symbolism The zinc house standing in a field of rubble Survival is arbitrary, not deserved
Pidgin English The thief leader's speech Gives the robbers a real voice and separates their world from Jonathan's formal English
Understatement The dead child mentioned in the same breath as the survivors The absence of visible grief conveys the scale of loss
Black humour The mispronunciation of ex-gratia as "egg-rasher" Laughter placed directly beside desperation
Contrast The family's shouting versus the total silence of the neighbourhood Shows the collapse of law and mutual protection
Circular structure The last paragraph returns to the first line's attitude Nothing has changed; the cycle of loss and work resumes
Two misreadings to avoid

(i) "Civil Peace" is not a simple happy story about optimism. Achebe's tone is ironic throughout, and the robbery is meant to disturb you. An answer that praises Jonathan's cheerfulness without noticing the irony is only half an answer. (ii) Do not say that the thieves are soldiers. The story never states who they are — the leader only says they are not as wicked as some others. The point is that the victim cannot tell, and that nobody comes when he calls.

5.7 Glossary

Word / phrase Meaning
civil war a war between groups inside the same country
Biafra the short-lived breakaway state in eastern Nigeria, 1967–70
inestimable too valuable to be measured
to commandeer to seize private property for official or military use
rubble broken pieces of stone and concrete left after a building falls
destitute extremely poor; having nothing at all
zinc (roof) a roof made of corrugated metal sheets
ex-gratia award a payment made as a favour, not because it is legally owed
"egg-rasher" the crowd's pronunciation of ex-gratia; the twenty-pound award
treasury the government office that holds and pays out public money
akara fried balls of ground bean paste, eaten in West Africa for breakfast
palm-wine an alcoholic drink made from the sap of palm trees
coal mine an underground works where coal is dug; Jonathan's old employer
Pidgin English a simplified mixed English used widely in Nigeria for daily speech
demobilised released from the army after a war
loot goods stolen, especially in wartime or disorder
vigil staying awake, usually at night, to watch or guard
verandah a roofed open platform along the outside of a house
miracle an event so lucky that it seems impossible
to shrug off to treat something bad as unimportant
Exam technique for this story

Almost every question on "Civil Peace" turns on the title. Whatever you are asked — about Jonathan, the thieves, the ending, the theme — make sure that somewhere in your answer you explain the irony of calling this "peace", and quote the thief's own line to prove it. Also learn the five blessings and the list of the family's occupations; short questions are often set directly on those details.

Chapter summary

  • Chinua Achebe (1930–2013), Nigerian, author of Things Fall Apart; "Civil Peace" comes from Girls at War and Other Stories (1972) and is set just after the Nigerian Civil War of 1967–70.
  • Jonathan Iwegbu counts five "inestimable blessings" — his own head, his wife Maria's and those of three of his four children — and repeats "Nothing puzzles God."
  • His buried bicycle survives the war; as a taxi it earns him a hundred and fifteen pounds in two weeks, which takes the family back to Enugu.
  • Their small zinc house still stands among ruins; the whole family works — mangoes, akara, a palm-wine bar — since the coal mine will not reopen.
  • At the treasury he receives a twenty-pound ex-gratia award, which the crowd calls "egg-rasher".
  • That night thieves knock; nobody answers the family's cries for help, and the leader mockingly calls for the police himself, saying "This time na Civil Peace."
  • Jonathan hands over the whole twenty pounds; by morning the family is back at work, and he says again that nothing puzzles God.
  • Themes: peace in name only, survival and work, loss, faith or fatalism, and the collapse of law and community; devices include irony, the repeated refrain, the bicycle as symbol, Pidgin English and a circular structure.

Practice questions

Short answer questions (2 marks each)

  1. What are Jonathan Iwegbu's five "inestimable blessings"? [2]
  2. Why does Jonathan treat his bicycle as a blessing, and how did he save it? [2]
  3. How does the Iwegbu family earn a living after they return to Enugu? [2]
  4. What is the "egg-rasher", and how much is it? [2]
  5. What happens when Jonathan's family shouts for help during the robbery? [2]
  6. How does Jonathan react to the loss of his money the next morning? [2]
Model answers — short questions

1. They are five heads that survived the war: his own, his wife Maria's, and those of three of his four children. The fourth child died. He counts survival itself as wealth, which shows both his gratitude and how much the war destroyed.

2. The bicycle is the machine that restarts his life: used as a taxi between the camps and the military cemetery, it earns him a hundred and fifteen pounds in two weeks. He saved it during the war by paying two pounds to an officer who wanted to commandeer it, and then burying it in the ground until the fighting was over.

3. Everyone works. Jonathan rides his bicycle as a taxi and later opens a bar selling palm-wine in his house; Maria makes and sells akara balls; and the children pick mangoes and sell them to soldiers' wives. His old job at the coal mine no longer exists.

4. It is the crowd's pronunciation of "ex-gratia award", a payment of twenty pounds made by the treasury to anyone who handed in the now worthless Biafran currency. Jonathan queues for his and receives it, and it is exactly this money the thieves demand that night.

5. Nothing happens. They call for neighbours, police and soldiers, and no one answers. The leader of the thieves then shouts for the police himself, in mockery, to prove to Jonathan that there is no help anywhere in the neighbourhood.

6. He refuses to be upset. He tells the sympathising neighbours not to trouble themselves, saying that the money came to him from nowhere only a few days before, so that losing it means nothing to him; and he repeats "Nothing puzzles God." He and his family are already back at work.

Long answer questions (5 marks each)

  1. Why is the story called "Civil Peace"? Discuss the irony of the title. [5]
  2. Sketch the character of Jonathan Iwegbu. Is his attitude to life admirable? [5]
  3. Discuss "Civil Peace" as a picture of a society just after a war. [5]
Model answers — long questions

1. The title is ironic from beginning to end. It comes from the thief himself, who tells Jonathan through the locked door that the civil war is finished and that this time it is "Civil Peace" — meaning that nobody need be killed provided the money is handed out. Achebe's point is that for ordinary Nigerians the end of the fighting brought a change of name rather than a change of condition. In the official version, peace has returned: the treasury is paying awards, offices are open, the government has won. In Jonathan's version, a man is robbed in the treasury queue, armed men knock at his door at night, and when his family screams for the police, the neighbours, and the soldiers, no one in the entire quarter answers. The thief even shouts for the police himself to prove the point. The irony is deepened by Jonathan's own language: he calls himself "extraordinarily lucky" when he has lost a child, a job and nearly all his property, and he describes the survival of five heads as inestimable blessings. In a genuine peace, none of this would be luck. The title therefore does exactly what a good title should: it states the official word for the situation and leaves the reader to discover what the word conceals.

2. Jonathan Iwegbu is a small man with an extraordinary capacity to begin again. Achebe shows him almost entirely through action. He bribes an officer to keep his bicycle and then buries it; he digs it up and has it earning money within days; he repairs a ruined house with wire and cardboard; he abandons the coal mine as soon as he sees the job will not return; he sets his wife and children to work; and when armed thieves come, he gives up everything rather than risk a life. His faith is of the same practical kind — "Nothing puzzles God" is less a doctrine than a refusal to be paralysed by what he cannot control. Much of this is admirable: his energy, independence and refusal of self-pity are exactly the qualities that rebuild a country, and Achebe clearly respects them. But the story also leaves room for doubt. Jonathan counts a dead son inside an arithmetic of blessings; he asks nobody for justice; he loses his award to criminals and by morning has decided that it does not matter. Endurance of that completeness may also be a kind of surrender, since a society in which everybody shrugs will never demand anything better. Achebe does not decide for us, and the best answers hold both views together.

3. Achebe's post-war Nigeria is drawn in a handful of exact details, and every one of them tells us something. Physically, the country is broken: houses lie in rubble, and Jonathan's flimsy zinc house survives when stronger ones did not, so that survival looks arbitrary rather than deserved. Economically, it is in collapse: the coal mine cannot say when it will reopen, the Biafran currency is waste paper, and the government's answer is a flat twenty-pound award for everyone. Whole families therefore live on tiny trades — mangoes, fried akara, palm-wine, a bicycle taxi that earns its money carrying people to and from a military cemetery. Socially, the most disturbing fact is the silence. The old protections have gone: no police come, no soldiers come, and the neighbours who will arrive at dawn to sympathise do not open a door at night. Violence has simply moved from the battlefield into the street, and its new practitioners are polite, organised and confident that nobody will stop them. Against all this Achebe sets the stubborn industry of one family. The picture that results is neither hopeless nor comfortable: people survive, but they survive alone, and the peace that has been declared protects nobody.

Reference to the context

  1. "Nothing puzzles God."

(a) Who says this, and when is it first said? (b) What does the speaker mean by it? (c) Where in the story is it repeated, and why is that placing important? (d) What does the line reveal about the speaker's character? [5]

  1. "No Civil War again. This time na Civil Peace."

(a) Who speaks these words, and to whom? (b) What is the situation at that moment? (c) Why is the sentence written in Pidgin English? (d) Explain the irony of the phrase and its link with the story's title. [5]

Model answers — reference to the context

1. (a) The words are Jonathan Iwegbu's, and they are first heard at the very beginning of the story, when he is counting the five "inestimable blessings" he has brought out of the civil war — his own head, his wife Maria's, and those of three of his four children. (b) He means that God's ways cannot be understood or questioned, so that whatever happens, good or bad, has to be accepted without complaint. (c) The same line closes the story, on the morning after the thieves have taken his entire twenty-pound award, when the neighbours come to sympathise. Placing it at both ends makes the story circular and shows that nothing has shaken him. (d) It reveals a man whose religion is entirely practical. He does not use it to explain the world but to avoid being destroyed by it; it is what allows him to stop grieving and start working again, and it is also, less comfortably, what allows him to demand nothing from anyone.

2. (a) They are spoken by the leader of the group of thieves, calling through the door to Jonathan Iwegbu at night. (b) The thieves have knocked and asked politely for the owner of the house; the family has screamed for neighbours, police and soldiers, and nobody has come — the leader has just mocked them by shouting for the police himself. He is now demanding a hundred pounds and assuring Jonathan that nobody need be hurt. (c) Achebe writes the thieves' speech in Nigerian Pidgin English because it is the real language of the street in that place and time. It makes the man immediately believable, and its casual, almost friendly tone against such a threat is far more frightening than shouting would be. (d) The irony is complete: the word "peace" is spoken by an armed robber, and what he means by it is only that he will not kill anyone if he is paid. It gives the story its title and states its theme — that the end of the war brought ordinary people a new name for their danger rather than safety from it.
